cells.tense: You are at the start of something and can hold its whole shape while you begin.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: Pick the smallest buildable job on the list this week and carry it right through to done — a repair, a page, supper for someone else — then let that person share in the finished thing.
cells.core:
You know how to begin. Something concrete is here worth giving form to, and you can hold the whole shape of it while you're still at the start — that's rare, and it's what this vantage is for. You don't need to see the finished version to trust the first move.

What's next that's concrete? Choose the smallest job you can actually carry through to done this week — a repair, a sketch, a page, supper for someone else — and take it all the way. Don't narrate it. Let it exist. The finished object will tell you more about what you can build than any plan would. Once you've done it, you'll know where the strength was.

cells.tense: The beginning hasn't happened yet and you're already bracing for what it will demand.
cells.act: name every feeling in it on one page, none of them crossed out
cells.ask: Give fifteen minutes to a single page about the thing you're bracing for — every part and feeling, all at once, named. No plan, no fix, nothing crossed out.
cells.core:
You are holding everything about this beginning that hasn't happened yet, and you're scanning the whole pattern, and you can't find a place to put your hand. The beginning is still ahead. It hasn't been written yet.

You can predict almost anything from the shape of it. That's the vantage working hard, not a flaw. But prediction turns to bracing the same way, and bracing makes the waiting heavier than the thing itself. So take it out of your head: name the whole of it, every part and feeling at once — no plan, no fix, nothing crossed out. The beginning doesn't need to be fully understood before it can be taken up. Bracing and beginning feel similar. They are not the same move.

cells.tense: That beginning is already behind you, and you haven't stepped through the door it was supposed to open.
cells.act: look at the whole of it until nothing is left to see
cells.ask: Take the next small step of something you've been avoiding and spread everything it actually involves on paper or the floor, so all of it sits in view together.
cells.core:
There's a beginning that already happened and you didn't step into it, and you're still at the door. The shape of it is mostly closed to you. The strength this vantage runs on isn't there right now, and it can't be forced.

Direct sight is the way through, small. Take the next small piece of something you've been avoiding, spread it out so the whole of it sits in view — the actual steps, not the story about them — and look until nothing is missing. Seeing it whole is enough for now. The door stays closed and that's fine. The whole shape can sit where you can look at it.

cells.tense: You can see whole situations before anyone else does, and you don't count it as yours.
cells.act: see it whole, with nothing hidden
cells.ask: When the whole picture arrives before anyone else's does, put a name on it — 'this is what I see' — before checking whether anyone would agree.
cells.core:
You can see the whole shape of something before anyone else at the table has started, and you have a habit of putting the pen down right after. You tell yourself you're keeping your head low. The others just call it quick.

You've been handing your reading off — calling it circumstance or group effort before it has a chance to be yours. Let it be complete once. When the whole picture arrives before anyone else's does, put a name on it before checking whether anyone would agree. What you can see is real and it is yours. Nobody has to sign off on it.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is 'and you keep watching anyway' in Too Much — the record doesn't say whether the person actually keeps watching or has turned away; I narrowed it to the watching itself, which is what Recognition is. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not always scanning; sometimes I'm just in it.' The asks survive: laying pieces out, naming feelings whole, doing one thing you can see finish, and taking the next piece of help are useful even if my read is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them is the Balanced closing move about trust — it praises my framing of the seat instead of handing them anything; I cut it.
